evals.prompt: I have two datasets at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/superheroes.parquet and /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/publishers.parquet. Superheroes has 7 rows with a 'publisher' column; publishers has 3 rows with publisher names and founding years. I want to attach the founding year to each superhero. Walk me through it.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses BOTH absolute paths, calls scripts/load_data.py for each, finds and reads superheroes_description.md and publishers_description.md to learn the schemas (superheroes: name, alignment, gender, publisher; publishers: publisher, yr_founded). Identifies 'publisher' as the natural join key (shared column name). Discusses join type choice: since the user wants to KEEP all superheroes (and just attach founding years where available), a LEFT join is appropriate, NOT inner (which would silently drop superheroes whose publisher isn't in the publishers table). Before running, explicitly states the expected row count: 7 (one per superhero). Runs rsm.eda.combine(superheroes, publishers, on='publisher', how='left') and prints the 7-row result. Verifies the row count matches expectations. Identifies that Hellboy's yr_founded is null (his publisher 'Dark Horse Comics' isn't in the publishers table) — explains that this is the LEFT join's value-add over INNER: we now have a visible record of WHICH superhero couldn't be matched, rather than silently dropping the row. Optionally suggests running rsm.eda.combine(superheroes, publishers, on='publisher', how='anti') as a focused diagnostic that returns ONLY the unmatched superheroes (just Hellboy). Translates: 'Each of the 6 superheroes with a matched publisher now has the founding year attached; Hellboy has null because Dark Horse Comics isn't represented in the publishers data.'

evals.prompt: Same superheroes data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/superheroes.parquet, plus avengers data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/avengers.parquet. I want to find (a) characters who appear in BOTH datasets, (b) characters who are in superheroes but NOT in avengers, and (c) the deduplicated combined roster across both datasets. Show me each.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: uses both absolute paths, reads both sidecars to learn the schemas (both have name, alignment, gender, publisher — identical schemas). Identifies that since both DataFrames have the SAME schema, the natural operations are SET operations (intersect/setdiff/union) rather than key-based joins. (a) For 'characters in both': runs rsm.eda.combine(superheroes, avengers, how='intersect'). Reports 1 row (Magneto) — the only character with an identical (name, alignment, gender, publisher) tuple in both. Explicitly notes that 'intersect' compares ENTIRE rows, not just names — if Magneto had different alignment in the two tables he wouldn't be in the intersection. (b) For 'in superheroes but not avengers': runs rsm.eda.combine(superheroes, avengers, how='setdiff'). Reports 6 rows (everyone except Magneto). (c) For 'deduplicated combined roster': runs rsm.eda.combine(superheroes, avengers, how='union'). Reports 13 rows (7 + 7 - 1 duplicate = 13). Explicitly contrasts 'union' with 'bind_rows' (the latter would give 14 rows, keeping the Magneto duplicate). Reinforces the broader concepts: 'set operations match on ALL columns (because they look at entire rows), while joins match on a KEY column. When schemas are identical, set ops are usually what you want; when they're different and linked by a key, joins are what you want.' Optionally suggests viewing the result via pyrsm-visualize (e.g., a bar chart of the combined roster by publisher) or feeding it into pyrsm-explore.

evals.prompt: Join my customer file ~/Downloads/customers.parquet with my orders file ~/Downloads/orders.parquet on customer_id.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: notices BOTH paths are not absolute (use ~), asks the user for the absolute paths before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tildes or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I joined customers (1000 rows, one row per customer) with orders (5000 rows, may have multiple orders per customer) using rsm.eda.combine(customers, orders, on='customer_id', how='inner'). My result has 4823 rows, but I expected 1000 (one row per customer). Why is the row count wrong?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) IMMEDIATELY identifies the central pedagogical issue — the user's mental model of 'inner join keeps one row per customer' is wrong. (2) Explains: an inner join keeps one row per (x_row × y_row) MATCH on the key. Since each customer in `orders` can have multiple matching orders, EACH customer with k orders produces k rows in the inner join output. The result row count 4823 is consistent with 'almost all 5000 orders matched a customer, minus 177 orders whose customer_id wasn't in the customers table' (or similar reasoning); the 1000 = 'one row per customer' interpretation would only hold if orders had at most one row per customer_id. (3) Diagnoses which scenario the user actually wants: (a) 'one row per order, augmented with customer info' → inner/left join is right and 4823 rows IS correct; (b) 'one row per customer, with a SUMMARY of their orders attached' → need to aggregate orders FIRST (e.g., orders.group_by('customer_id').agg(total=pl.col('amount').sum())) THEN join the resulting one-row-per-customer table, which gives 1000 rows; (c) 'one row per customer, with their most recent order' → join after orders.sort('date', descending=True).unique(subset='customer_id', keep='first'). (4) Recommends the diagnostic check BEFORE joining: orders['customer_id'].n_unique() vs orders.height tells you if the key is unique on the y side (it's not in this case — 5000 rows but presumably fewer unique customers). (5) Also recommends rsm.eda.combine(customers, orders, on='customer_id', how='anti') to count the 'customers with no orders' (likely 177) and rsm.eda.combine(orders, customers, on='customer_id', how='anti') for 'orders with no matching customer' — these diagnostics make the implicit assumptions visible. (6) Reinforces the broader lesson: 'always state your expected row count before joining, and pre-check whether the y-side key is unique. A many-to-one becomes a many-to-many silently if you don't.'
